title: Node rescue and capacity top-up runbook (wip)
content:
Purpose: quick-reference runbook for rescuing a degraded node (GPU hardware or driver issues), performing a safe cordon/drain, applying a temporary heterogeneous backfill, and rehydrating caches/kv stores so serving SLAs recover with minimal request loss. This is a working doc — fill in cluster-specific IDs and region tags during incident.

When to use this:
- Node shows repeated GPU ECC errors, driver panics, or GPU kernel OOMs.
- Node Ready toggles to NotReady after transient repair attempts.
- Immediate capacity shortage causing request queueing and elevated latency that cannot be solved by autoscaler fast-path.

Safety prechecks (first 5 minutes):
- Pager escalation: if > 10% tail latency increase or error-rate > 3x baseline for 5m, notify SRE lead and Product Oncall.
- Check cluster health: kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "NotReady|Unknown"
- Confirm pods affected: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Failed OR describe pods on the impacted nodes.
- GPU health: ssh to node (if allowed) and check nvidia-smi, /var/log/messages and dmesg for ECC or reset events.
  - nvidia-smi -q | egrep "Ecc|Xid|Reset"
  - journalctl -k | egrep "NVRM|GPU|nvlink"

Decision: repair in-place vs replace node
- If driver can be recovered within 15 min with a safe restart (no sustained kernel panics) and there is spare capacity, attempt in-place: restart nvidia-driver, kubelet restart, test with a synthetic GPU job.
- If multiple XID errors, persistent machine-level panics, or hardware swap required -> Replace node and backfill.

In-place quick repair (if chosen):
1) Cordon node: kubectl cordon NODE_NAME
2) Restart kubelet and driver: sudo systemctl restart nvidia-docker.service || sudo systemctl restart nvidia-persistenced && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
3) Run a small test container that uses the GPU: kubectl run gpu-test --image=nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:11.8-base --restart=Never --command -- sleep 60 --requests=nvidia.com/gpu=1 --limits=nvidia.com/gpu=1 -n staging-test
4) Monitor logs for 5–10m. If no errors, uncordon: kubectl uncordon NODE_NAME.

Replace node + capacity top-up (preferred if hardware suspected):
1) Mark node unschedulable: kubectl taint node NODE_NAME rescue=true:NoSchedule --overwrite
2) Drain gracefully: kubectl drain NODE_NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
   - If critical pods with PodDisruptionBudget block drains, escalate to product oncall for permission to violate PDBs. Document PDB name and owner.
3) Trigger replacement: follow infra provider playbook (cloud console or metal ops): - Create replacement node with tag: redwood-rescue, region, gpu-type=<backfill-gpu> (see hetero guidance below).
4) If using heterogeneous backfill (e.g., different GPU model), label node: kubectl label node NEW_NODE gpu.backfill=true gpu.type=rtx-a5000 (or appropriate)
5) Add node to serving pool: remove NoSchedule taint and allow pod-scheduling.

Workload hints for heterogenous backfills:
- Avoid scheduling long-lived KV-cache rehydration jobs onto mismatched GPU types. Use nodeSelector or node affinity to keep cache warmers on original pool where possible.
- For serving pods, prefer starting a small fraction (10–20%) of replicas on the new node type to validate behavior. Use a rollout or manual placement.
- If model quantization differences matter (FP16 vs INT8), ensure model variant compatible with GPU. If not, route traffic to compatible variants until migration is done.

Cache/KV rehydration and warmup steps (important to restore latency quickly):
- Identify critical caches on the drained node (prefix caches, kv-store shards).
  - Query Redis/etcd topology and find keys with node affinity.
  - Run a targeted warmup job that replays recent hot prefixes (from traces): python scripts/rehydrate_hot_prefixes.py --keys-file hot-prefixes-NODE_NAME.txt --parallel=8
- If using local disco cache on node (memcache), accept some cold misses; start warmers at low QPS and ramp.

Traffic routing and SLO safety gates:
- If overall error rate or 95th latency remain > SLO after replacements, enable routing fallback: update routing policy to point traffic to low-latency region or dedicated pool (see routing playbook).
- Do not trigger global fallback unless incident commander authorizes.

Commands cheat-sheet:
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe node NODE_NAME
- kubectl cordon NODE_NAME; kubectl drain NODE_NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
- kubectl uncordon NODE_NAME
- kubectl label node NODE_NAME key=value --overwrite

Rollback criteria:
- If new node causes unexpected errors (GPU driver incompat, scheduler evictions), cordon it immediately and rollback label/taint changes. Use: kubectl cordon NEW_NODE; kubectl drain NEW_NODE --delete-local-data --force; then deprovision via infra ticket.

Post-incident activities (required):
- Capture timeline in incident doc: who, what, when, decision points, mitigations. Link to JIRA.
- Run a short postmortem within 72 hours if user impact > 30 minutes or > 5% customer requests failed.
- Update this runbook with exact playbook commands used (replace placeholders) and any tuned thresholds.
- Schedule a follow-up to evaluate inventory: how many similar nodes exist (same firmware/driver) and whether batch replacements are warranted.

Notes to self / open questions (fill during runbook iteration):
- Add exact command for our infra provider to provision a node with a specific GPU SKU (cloud CLI or metal ops script).
- Add automatic metric check script to detect ECC XID trends and create a remediation alert pipeline.

Acceptance criteria for runbook completion:
- We validated heterogeneous backfill path in staging (test cluster) with at least one model and one cache warmer.
- Documented rollback steps are tested and timed under 15 minutes.

Appendix: useful links and quick refs:
- GPU health dashboard (grafana): https://grafana.redwood.company/d/gpu-health
- Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.company/sre/incident-template
- Jira epic for capacity automation: JIRA-SRE-2127

End of doc — please add notes from real incidents below as examples so new oncall can learn.
